title: India Tells Washington: We Do Not Have Overcapacity in Anything. The Section 301 Fight Is Just Beginning.
excerpt: India's trade secretary rejects US allegations of structural excess capacity in textiles and steel, days before Modi and Trump are expected to meet at the G7
body:
India's top trade official delivered a blunt rebuttal to Washington's accusations of industrial overcapacity this week, dismissing the charge as a misreading of what the world's most populous country actually needs.

"Overcapacity is a country's perspective. We don't think we have overcapacity in anything," said Amitabh Kumar, India's additional trade secretary, responding to allegations in the U.S. Trade Representative's Section 301 investigation that India maintains structural excess capacity in industries from textiles and steel to solar modules and petrochemicals.

The exchange matters because it lands days before Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to sit across from President Donald Trump at the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France, where trade will be one of the most contentious items on the agenda.

## 'How Do We Have Overcapacity?'

Kumar's argument was rooted in per capita consumption — a framing that highlights the gulf between how Washington and New Delhi view the same data. India produces large quantities of textiles and steel in absolute terms, but its per capita consumption of both remains among the lowest in the world.

"This country has a hot climate, tropical climate. We wear cotton. How do we have overcapacity?" Kumar said, noting that India's textile output per person was very low, particularly in man-made fibre and technical textiles.

On steel, Kumar pointed out that India's per capita consumption places it well below the global average, even as the country has become the world's second-largest producer. "India's per capita steel consumption is among the lowest," he said, adding that production reflects the country's development requirements, not surplus dumping.

## The Section 301 Shadow

The stakes are higher than a diplomatic argument. In March, the office of the USTR launched investigations against India and 15 other countries over policies it alleges allow factories to keep producing beyond what market conditions support. Washington cited India's $42 billion goods trade surplus with the United States in 2025 as evidence.

Trade analysts say the real pressure points are elsewhere. Washington is using the threat of Section 301 tariffs to press India to open its agricultural markets, purchase more American energy and defence products, and address concerns around intellectual property and data localisation.

The threat is not theoretical. Washington has proposed an additional 12.5 per cent tariff on imports from India and several other countries, alleging the use of forced labour — a charge India has flatly rejected.

## The Trade Deal Window

Despite the tensions, both sides are talking about a breakthrough. U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said earlier this month that a deal could come in "the not-too-distant future." India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said the two countries were negotiating a "fair, equitable and balanced agreement" and that a first tranche could be concluded by mid-July.

India is pushing for preferential tariff treatment over competitors, while the U.S. wants greater market access for agricultural products, Harley-Davidson motorcycles, dairy, and stricter commitments on IP rights.

A State Bank of India report underscores the shifting dynamics. Between April and July 2025, the U.S. trade deficit with India actually widened from $17 billion to $23 billion — even as Washington's overall trade deficit shrank. India is becoming more important to American trade, not less, and that gives New Delhi leverage it did not have a decade ago.

## The Diaspora Stakes

For NRIs working in Indian pharmaceutical exports, textile companies with American clients, and IT firms navigating the trade landscape, the outcome of these negotiations will shape the business environment for years. A deal that secures preferential tariffs could accelerate India's emergence as a post-China manufacturing hub. A breakdown could mean higher costs, supply chain disruptions, and a more hostile regulatory environment in the United States.

Modi and Trump will have roughly 90 minutes together on the sidelines in Évian. The overcapacity debate will be one of many items on the table. But Kumar's public rebuttal this week signals that India is not walking into those talks willing to concede the premise.

Sources: Reuters, The Indian Eye, SBI Research, LiveMint
